name: Karl Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play bass on paid studio tracks, lead a weekend trio and teach six guitar pupils. I have a music degree, yet the skill clients mention is that I can take a rough singer’s idea and make it sit in a live band.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I send the finished invoice, then help get our two children ready for school. My partner has a salaried clinic job, and we keep a mortgage calendar and a separate account for quieter months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the trio that a faster booking email is fine, but an audience still hears us together. I would keep the Saturday sets that pay and the studio clients who ask for a real bass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have eleven months of household expenses saved and I earn well for a working musician. One dry month would not frighten me, although the mortgage still arrives on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep my six pupils, paid studio sessions and Saturday trio nights. I already use AI every day to sort practice recordings; I listen to every clip before a pupil sees a comment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this picture. It changes a little paperwork without taking away the paid work I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a Saturday night worth accepting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The venue must write down the fee and finish time, because our pickup arrangement ends at a set hour. I would ask for those terms before adding a new date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever send an unchecked AI note to a child?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A tidy comment on a bad guitar recording can still teach a child the wrong thing. I listen to the clip and write the final note myself.

say: I would welcome **faster booking emails** while keeping live paid sets.
I would demand **written venue terms** before taking extra Saturdays.
think: Our **eleven-month reserve** can cover one dry month.
The **mortgage** still makes actual paid dates more useful than a promising invitation.
do: Keep **six pupils**, paid studio sessions and Saturday trio nights this month.
Request **written fees** and finish times before accepting extra venue dates.
feel: I feel **calm** because current paid work looks secure.
S0.quote: A tidy comment on a bad guitar recording can still teach a child the wrong thing.
fieldNote: His **strong cushion** and several paid streams support calm in the plateau.
His **daily AI sorting** is existing use, with his own listening before pupil feedback.

steps.text: Keep six guitar pupils, paid studio sessions and Saturday trio nights
Request written venue fee and finish time before accepting extra dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell studio clients that cheaper generated bass lines will arrive before any robot carries an amplifier. I would ask for real recording dates and clear cancellation fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Studio tracks are roughly a third of my own pay, and some clients will try generated takes. The trio and pupils still pay, but I cannot assume they replace every session.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask the studio for a written schedule of paid sessions and its cancellation terms. In the first year I would take the engineer’s paid lesson on a new stem-separation tool, which splits a recording into instrument parts, then test my own unlabelled bass take only if storage stays in the studio; I would compare it by ear with the original and stop if timing shifts or the file leaves that room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about the recording fees. Being early with a tool does not make a client owe me a session.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could a pupil’s recording be your test file?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I will not upload a child’s voice or name to that tool; my own bass take is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the written studio schedule is short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If paid sessions actually shrink, I would apply for a posted house-band bass seat. I would check the written net fee after travel and a finish time compatible with child pickup before taking it.

say: I would request **written recording dates** and cancellation terms.
I would take **paid engineer instruction** before testing the cleaner.
think: Generated tracks could remove about **one-third** of my pay.
The **trio and pupils** may not replace all lost studio sessions.
do: Request a **written studio schedule** and cancellation terms next month.
Test the **new stem tool** after paid instruction on my nameless take; compare by ear and stop on timing or storage failure.
Apply for a **posted bass seat** if paid sessions shrink, only with suitable written net fee and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about realistic studio income loss.
S1.quote: Being early with a tool does not make a client owe me a session.
fieldNote: His **new tool trial** requires paid instruction, his own unlabelled recording, in-studio storage and ear comparison.
A **house-band move** requires actual lost sessions, a posted paid opening, better net fee and pickup-compatible finish.

steps.text: Test studio stem tool after paid lesson on own take; listen, stop on errors or leakage
Apply for posted bass seat if sessions shrink, net fee and pickup fit
Keep paid trio nights and six pupils while studio calls remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the studio owner that AGI by 2028 could supply a finished bass track cheaply. I would ask which live sessions and trio dates are actually contracted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most studio sessions to disappear in 2028, and some venues may choose generated backing tracks too. Playing robots arrive around 2031, three years later; I can lose a third of my pay before a robot learns the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would total the studio invoices and request a written trio calendar. In the first year after 2028, if paid trio nights also fall, I would apply for a posted school ensemble-tutor job only if my degree qualifies, its written net pay after travel replaces the lost gigs and pickup works; I would keep pupils and trio work until a signed offer has hours and pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed if sessions and venue dates both fell, because together that is nearly half my own income. I have lain awake counting how many mortgage payments eleven months of savings really buys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy expensive sound gear to compete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not on a guess. I would keep six months of expenses untouched and buy gear only after a signed paid recording order covers its cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school tutor post is only a tip from a friend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working until the school posts it and gives me written hours. A friendly tip does not pay the mortgage.

say: I would ask for **contracted live dates** before planning household evenings.
I would seek a **posted tutor vacancy** if paid trio nights fall.
think: Most **studio fees** could disappear with AGI in 2028.
Further lost **trio nights** could make the hit nearly half my pay before 2031 robots.
do: Count **studio invoices** and request a written trio calendar now.
Apply for a **posted tutor post** after 2028 trio cuts only if qualified, net pay replaces gigs and pickup fits.
Keep **pupils and trio work** until a suitable signed offer states hours and pay.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected large losses and mortgage worry.
S2.quote: I can lose a third of my pay before a robot learns the stairs.
fieldNote: He expects **studio income loss** in 2028, before capable playing robots around 2031.
The **school route** needs real trio cuts, a posted job, degree eligibility, written net pay, pickup and signed hours.

steps.text: Apply after 2028 trio cuts for posted qualifying tutor role with replacement written net-after-travel and pickup
Keep pupils and paid trio work until suitable signed offer states hours and pay
Protect six months of household expenses while searching
Buy recording gear only after signed paid recording order covers its cost

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the venue owner that five years before AGI by 2031 gives us time to build an event people buy tickets for. I would try one paid bass-and-drums workshop, with players who are paid to teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Studio sessions may end by 2031, but a workshop can earn its own fee if adults actually book. Playing robots arrive around 2034, so I would test the demand before treating live performance as safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would book one Sunday workshop only if the venue gives a room after our children’s pickup, twelve adults prepay enough for the room, safe loan instruments, the drummer’s fee and my teaching fee. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat only if those twelve paid places and the room remain, instruments pass inspection and pickup still fits; I would keep the six guitar pupils either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about studio income shrinking while I test whether workshops pay. I can risk a small pilot because we have savings. I will not ask a workshop drummer to teach for publicity instead of pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who inspects the loan instruments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The venue technician would check amps, cables and drums before participants touch them. If inspection fails, we use participants’ safe instruments or cancel the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if seven adults prepay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seven tickets will not cover both teachers and the room. I would refund the tickets and keep the regular trio booking instead.

say: I would trial a **paid workshop** with both teachers paid.
I would refund **seven tickets** if they cannot cover the full cost.
think: A **paid workshop** could replace some studio fees if twelve adults book.
**Playing robots** follow AGI around 2034, so live demand still needs testing.
do: Start a **Sunday workshop** only with twelve prepayments covering room, inspected gear and both teachers after pickup.
Repeat the **paid workshop** after 2031 only with twelve fees covering room and both teachers, inspected gear and pickup.
Keep **six guitar pupils** if the workshop cannot pay both teachers.
feel: I feel **anxious** because studio fees could shrink while paid workshops are tested.
S3.quote: I will not ask a workshop drummer to teach for publicity instead of pay.
fieldNote: The **workshop pilot** requires twelve prepaid adults, a room after pickup and fees for both teachers.
The technician must **inspect equipment**; unsafe gear means participant instruments or cancellation.

steps.text: Start workshop if twelve prepay room and both teachers, gear passes inspection and pickup fits
Renew after 2031 if twelve prepay costs, room and safe gear remain, pickup fits
Keep six guitar pupils if workshop fees fail

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that a decade before AGI by 2036 is room to learn and earn, not a reason to stop playing now. A booking is real only when the fee and the finish time are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Studio pay may fall by 2036 and live venues might face robots around 2039. I would rather build a paid teaching route while the trio still has bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would take a funded evening certificate in school music leadership only if there is a place and my partner can cover pickup without losing clinic pay. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for a posted school music coordinator job only if the certificate and degree qualify me, its written net pay after travel covers lost studio fees and pickup fits; I would keep paid trio work and pupils until a signed offer states hours and pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about later income, but I have time and a reserve to make a careful move. I would not call the course a solution until a paid vacancy exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the certificate loses funding, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid gigs and pupils and wait for another funded place. I will not take tuition out of the six months I want untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept an impressive title with lower pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The written net pay has to cover what I lose from studio work after travel, or the title is just a label.

say: I would seek a **funded certificate** only if pickup does not cost clinic pay.
I would require a **written school offer** before leaving paid music work.
think: My **studio pay** may fall by 2036 before 2039 playing robots.
A **school route** helps only if a qualified paid opening actually exists.
do: Take a **funded leadership certificate** only with an actual place and pickup without lost partner pay.
Apply for a **posted coordinator job** after 2036 only if qualified, written net pay covers studio loss and pickup fits.
Keep **paid trio work** and pupils until a suitable signed offer states hours and pay.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant income loss while I can prepare.
S4.quote: A booking is real only when the fee and the finish time are written down.
fieldNote: His **funded certificate** requires a real place and child pickup without reducing his partner’s pay.
The **school move** needs a qualified posted opening, written net pay, pickup and a signed offer before leaving music work.

steps.text: Take funded music-leadership certificate only with place and pickup without lost clinic pay
Apply after 2036 for posted qualifying coordinator role with written net-after-travel covering studio loss and pickup
Keep paid trio and pupils until suitable signed offer states hours and pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because studio fees and live nights could fall together. Signed venue dates, a real posted school job and pickup that does not cost my partner a shift would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the drummer after a workshop. If I cannot pay the workshop's drummer, I have not built a business.

headlineQuote: If I cannot pay the workshop's drummer, I have not built a business.
portrait: At **43**, Karl is an experienced bassist with a music degree, two children, a mortgage and eleven months saved.
His higher **musician pay** comes from studio tracks, a weekend trio and six guitar pupils.
He uses **AI daily**, yet tests a new studio tool only after paid instruction, ear checks and in-studio storage.
He would build a **paid workshop** only when twelve adults cover the room, safe gear and both teaching fees.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove studio sessions and reduce paid trio nights together.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed venue dates**, a real school vacancy and pickup without lost clinic pay would help Karl.
